newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: WorldCom gets licence for Zurich cable.
newsitem.headline: WorldCom gets licence for Zurich cable.

text.p: WorldCom Inc, the U.S. communications provider, said on Monday it had received a licence to build and operate an alternative municipal telecommunications network in Zurich.
WorldCom said it already has a licence for public telecommunications services in Switzerland, and since January 1996 has provided non-infrastructural services in voice and data.
The licence entitles WorldCom to construct, or use existing public facilities to build, its high-speed, totally fibre optic-based SDH (synchronous digital hierarchy) network.
It said the project would be coordinated by an affiliate, MKI, and will include local construction firms.
Patrick Moser, managing director for WorldCom Schweiz, told Reuters the overall investment amount would be between 20 and 30 million Swiss francs ($13.2 million to $19.8 million).
The cost of work by subcontractors was expected to be around three million francs, the company said in a statement.
Installation is to begin in mid-September and the network is expected to be completed by the first quarter of 1998.
WorldCom also said that a competitor, COLT Telecommunications, had been granted a similar licence.

WorldCom expected its network, aimed mainly at business customers, to be hooked up to over 200 buildings in the city of Zurich, giving some 10,000 employees in those buildings direct access to over 20,000 buildings served by WorldCom worldwide.
WorldCom said it currently has municipal networks in 47 cities worldwide.

WorldCom said the move was also a sign of impending liberalisation in Switzerland's communications industry, now dominated by the Swiss government's Telecom PTT. The government plans to float part of its stake in Telecom in the second half of 1998, the year when extensive telecom deregulation is slated within the European Union in 1998.

Moser said the decision to grant WorldCom the licence for the new network was ground-breaking. It included permission from the Swiss Federal Office of Communications (BAKOM) providing the company with a special concession, as well as the decision by Zurich authorities to allow it to set up the network.
"In this combination we can operate like a liberalised telecom," said Moser.
The company said in its statement that further expansion would depend on demand.
